title: Writing on the forehead
hookLine: a receipt in a coat pocket, a record no one else can read: the Oankar on what is written, and Japji on the deeds that write it

lines: A RECEIPT IN AN OLD COAT.
cards: A coat comes out of the closet after a long summer, and in the pocket there's a receipt: coffee for two, a date, a time. Faded, but still there. Nobody meant to keep it.

It's a small record of something that actually happened. There's an old way of speaking about the record of a life: what's written on the forehead. The Oankar picks up that old picture of writing, and so does the Japji.
Put the two side by side and a question comes up: who holds the pen?

teach.b: Start with the Oankar. In one stanza, Guru Nanak speaks to a friend, sakhi, and says, in paraphrase: the writing does not get erased, the writing the Creator has written.
What is written cannot be turned back; as it pleases You, so take care of it. The word for that writing is lekh. On its own, that could sound like a locked door: everything decided, nothing to do.
But the same stanza ends, in paraphrase: by Your glance of grace, peace is found, reflecting on the Word.
Grace is in the room. Now turn to the Japji. There Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: being called virtuous or sinful is not just talk.
The actions you do, again and again, are written down, and you carry them with you. You sow, and you eat what you sow. Here the pen is in our own hand.

Not one big deed, but karna, doing, repeated, until it becomes the record. So the scripture holds three things together: the Creator's writing, our own deeds writing day after day, and grace that can arrive.
Sikh readers explain how these fit in more than one way, and this path won't settle it for them. But the picture is clear enough for a Tuesday.

teach.h: PART OF IT IS WRITTEN TODAY.
teach.b: A record is being kept, and part of it is being written right now by what we actually do.
Not by what we meant, or said we'd do. The receipt in the coat pocket was printed by a real afternoon.

how: In Sikh teaching, lekh, what is written, is spoken of alongside karam, deeds, and nadar, grace; some teachers present it less as fate to wait out than as a reason for honest work and seva.

games.q: what does “writing on the forehead” mean?
o: a mark painted on the brow at worship
a fate fixed so nothing we do matters
the record of a life, written by deeds too

games.q: what's written, and where — tap the pairs.
p: the Creator's writing is not erased
friend: who the Oankar line speaks to

s: in the Oankar, what is written leaves no room for grace
the same stanza ends on grace: by Your glance, peace is found, reflecting on the Word.
the Japji says virtue and sin are not just talk
the deeds you do again and again are written down, and you carry them.

games.q: you've read that what's written can't be erased. where does that Oankar stanza end?
o: on grace: by Your glance, peace is found.
tell the friend to stop reading.
games.why: the stanza that says the writing can't be erased ends on grace: by Your glance, peace is found, reflecting on the Word.

practice: Let one person come to mind who could use something small from you, a message, a ride, a meal, a thank-you, and pick one thing plain enough to finish before tonight. See yourself doing it, start to end, then rest with the breath.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out; if not, let the choice settle quietly, like ink drying.

wordCard.voice: Writing on the forehead. The lekh, the record of a life: in the Oankar, the Creator's writing; in the Japji, deeds done again and again, written down and carried. Today's word.

orig.note: lekh: the writing, the record; in the Oankar, the writing the Creator has written.

carryVoice: Your line: what's written. Part of today's page is still blank. Take care today.

sources.ref: Ramkali, Mahala 1, Dakhni Oankar ('lekh na mittaee he sakhee jo likhiaa kartaar'; 'nadar teree sukh paaiaa naanak sabad veechaar'), Ang 937
Japji, pauri 20 ('punnee paapee aakhan naahi, kar kar karnaa likh lai jaahu'), Ang 4
